strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem: the high latency and storage costs of multi-vector ColPali-style multimodal retrievers, and proposes a lightweight test-time method (GQR) that uses a complementary dense text retriever's scores to refine the primary retriever's query embedding.

The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: the three-level taxonomy of hybrid aggregation (ranking / score / representation) is a useful framing, and GQR elegantly exploits gradient access to the primary retriever's representation space while remaining architecture-agnostic across single- and multi-vector retrievers.

The evaluation is extensive and thorough: 9 retriever pairs across ViDoRe 1 and ViDoRe 2, comparison against 8 hybrid baselines (including tuned variants), a comparison against a multimodal cross-encoder reranker (MonoQwen2-VL), and careful latency and storage measurements on identical hardware.

The Pareto-frontier analysis (Figures 2, 3, 5) convincingly supports the central efficiency claim: Colnomic-7B with GQR nearly matches or exceeds Llama-Nemo-3B while being ~7-14x faster and requiring ~24-54x less memory.

The paper includes several informative ablations (extra search stage, candidate pool policy, loss function choice, role swapping) that increase confidence in design choices and reveal honest findings (e.g., gains are largely confined to the initial candidate pool; ViDoRe 1 is saturated and shows no benefit).
Code release is promised, and implementation details (hyperparameter grids, tuning protocol, Docling ingestion, K=10) are documented sufficiently for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is a fairly direct adaptation of established test-time query optimization / pseudo-relevance feedback ideas (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025) from the cross-encoder-to-bi-encoder distillation setting, here replacing the cross-encoder guidance with a complementary bi-encoder and a KL-to-consensus objective. The conceptual contribution, while sensible, is incremental.

Absolute gains are modest and inconsistent: average NDCG@5 improvements of +0.7 to +4.0 points on ViDoRe 2, with some subset-level degradations (e.g., Colnomic-7B with Qwen3 on Biomed Lectures -2.4), and essentially no benefit on ViDoRe 1. No statistical significance testing is reported, so the reliability of small deltas is unclear.

GQR requires per-subset, in-domain hyperparameter tuning (learning rate and T tuned on 10% of each subset), which the authors acknowledge limits zero-shot applicability. The tuned baselines receive the same tuning, but the practical deployment cost of this tuning protocol deserves more discussion.

Evaluation is confined to the ViDoRe benchmark family with English documents and small corpora (page-level retrieval); generalization to other domains, languages, larger-scale corpora, or non-document retrieval tasks is untested.
The method is limited to M=2 retrievers in practice, and there is no analysis of how gains scale with the number of complementary retrievers despite the formulation claiming generality.

Some claims are slightly stronger than the evidence: the statement that GQR 'pushes the Pareto frontier' holds on these benchmarks with the specific model set, but the headline figures (14x faster, 54x less memory) depend on the choice of a particularly expensive baseline (Llama-Nemo) and are not uniform across configurations.

Latency overhead of GQR varies considerably by complementary retriever (65ms to 343ms added latency; up to ~300% overhead for the smallest base latency of ~116ms for Colnomic), which somewhat tempers the 'lightweight' framing in the abstract.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: the high memory and latency cost of multi-vector ColPali-style retrievers, and proposes a lightweight test-time mechanism (GQR) to fuse a weak text retriever's signal into a stronger vision retriever's query embedding.

The empirical study is fairly broad: 9 vision-text model pairs, two benchmark families (ViDoRe 1 and 2), 8 hybrid baselines including tuned score-fusion variants, a comparison against a multimodal reranker (MonoQwen2-VL), and latency/storage measurements on real hardware.

Useful ablations are provided: extra search stage, candidate pool policy, alternative losses (JS, KL-target), and role swapping of primary/complementary retrievers (Table 17), which reveal that even weaker retrievers can provide useful guidance.

The writing is generally clear, the method is architecture-agnostic and easy to follow (Algorithm 1), and the Pareto-frontier framing of latency vs. quality vs. storage is a sensible way to present the results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. GQR is a straightforward adaptation of existing test-time query optimization / pseudo-relevance feedback work (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025) that simply swaps the cross-encoder guidance signal for a weaker bi-encoder's scores and applies KL minimization to the query embedding on a small candidate pool. The core mechanism is an incremental combination of known ideas, and the paper offers no theoretical grounding (acknowledged in the Limitations).

Gains are modest and benchmark-dependent. On ViDoRe 2, GQR's average gain (+3.9%) is only marginally above the tuned Score Aggregation (Min-Max) baseline (+3.4%) and tuned SoftMax aggregation (+2.6%), with no statistical significance testing anywhere in the paper. On ViDoRe 1 the method provides essentially no benefit (−0.1% on average, Table 7), so the headline claims rest almost entirely on a single benchmark.

Concerning evaluation protocol. Hyperparameters (T, α) are tuned per dataset-subset on a 10% dev split selected by NDCG@5, while baseline tuned variants get only a single weight α. This asymmetric tuning effort may favor GQR, and per-subset in-domain tuning undermines the claimed practicality (the Limitations concede this is not a zero-shot method).

The headline efficiency claims (14x faster, 54x less memory) are misleading framing: these numbers compare Colnomic+GQR against Llama-Nemo, a specific and unusually expensive competitor, rather than reflecting what GQR itself contributes; against other baselines the latency overhead of GQR is a real cost, and the paper's strongest absolute results (e.g., rerankers at k=10/20 in Table 9) actually outperform GQR at the cost of latency.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only the ViDoRe benchmarks, no external datasets or out-of-domain stress tests (GQR is explicitly tuned in-domain), and several individual configurations show GQR harming performance (e.g., Qwen3 as complementary model), suggesting sensitivity to retriever pairing that is not well characterized.

Some presentation issues: Table 1 vs. Table 8/9 report slightly inconsistent figures for the same configurations, and the main text (Sec 3.2) states 65.2 while Table 8 reports 65.15 and Table 9 65.15/65.1 for the same setting; such sloppiness erodes confidence in the numbers.

strengths: The core idea of Guided Query Refinement is well-motivated and clearly positioned: the paper connects hybrid retrieval with test-time query optimization and proposes operating between score-level and representation-level aggregation, which is a genuinely under-explored design point. The formulation (minimizing KL between the primary retriever's distribution and a consensus distribution) is clean, architecture-agnostic, and applicable to both single- and multi-vector retrievers.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: 9 vision-text model pairs across 3 ColPali-based and 3 text retrievers, 8 hybrid baselines (including tuned variants), two benchmark suites (ViDoRe 1 and 2), two metrics (NDCG@5, Recall@5), and extensive ablations (extra search stage, candidate pool policy, loss function choice, role swapping). This is more comprehensive than typical for retrieval papers.

The efficiency analysis is a real strength: latency and storage measurements on identical hardware, Pareto-frontier plots, and the headline result that a Colnomic+GQR hybrid nearly matches LLAMA-NEMO at ~14x faster and ~54x less memory is practically significant and well supported (Table 8, Figures 2 and 5).
The comparison against a cross-encoder reranker (MonoQwen2-VL) at matched candidate settings is a fair and informative baseline that many papers omit.
The finding that a much weaker complementary retriever (e.g., Qwen3, 16.2 points below Llama-Nemo) can still improve the strongest model via GQR is an interesting and non-obvious empirical insight.

Hyperparameter search spaces, dev/test splits, and implementation details (Docling version, RRF constant, optimizer choice) are documented well enough for reasonable reproducibility, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are modest and inconsistent: +3.9% average on ViDoRe 2 over the base retriever is small in absolute NDCG terms (typically +1-4 points), and the method is essentially neutral on ViDoRe 1 (deltas of -0.2 to +0.1, Table 7). The paper attributes ViDoRe 1's flatness to saturation, which is plausible but weakens the evidence that GQR is broadly beneficial rather than benchmark-specific.

The margin over the strongest baseline is thin: tuned Score Aggregation (Min-Max) achieves +3.4% vs. GQR's +3.9%, and on some subsets (e.g., Biomed Lectures, Economics) the tuned baselines are close or better. No statistical significance testing or variance analysis is provided, so it is hard to judge whether GQR reliably outperforms the tuned score-aggregation baselines rather than being within noise.

GQR (and the tuned baselines) require per-subset hyperparameter tuning on an in-domain dev set (10% of each subset). This weakens the zero-shot/deployment story compared to untuned RRF, and the paper does not report sensitivity of results to the dev-set size or to hyperparameter choices (the T and alpha grids are given but no ablation on their effect is shown).

The method is close to prior test-time query optimization work (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025), with the main delta being the replacement of a cross-encoder guide with a complementary bi-encoder. The novelty is real but incremental; a deeper analysis of why bi-encoder guidance works (e.g., what properties of the refined embedding change, or theoretical grounding) is limited to ablation tables, and the paper itself acknowledges the treatment is purely empirical.

Latency numbers depend on implementation and hardware (single A100, batching choices), and the 14x/54x headline figures are relative to a particularly expensive model (Llama-Nemo with 10.6 MB/page); relative to more typical configurations the efficiency advantage would be smaller. The claim 'up to 14x faster' could be misread as a general result.

Scale of experiments is limited to ViDoRe 1/2 (4-10 subsets each, mostly English, financial/technical documents). Generalization to other domains, languages, or larger-scale corpora (where ANN search behavior differs from exhaustive scoring over small candidate pools) is untested.

Some presentation issues: results for ViDoRe 2 in Table 1 vs. Table 14/16 differ slightly (e.g., 65.2 vs. 65.1 for Llama-Nemo+Linq), suggesting different runs or configurations without explanation; Figure 1's caption has a grammatical error ('a complementary retriever'); and the headline claims in the abstract lean on the most favorable configuration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: improving multimodal (ColPali-style) retrieval with lightweight text retrievers while keeping latency and storage low is practically relevant, and the paper is well positioned within the hybrid retrieval and test-time query refinement literatures.

The proposed method (GQR) is simple, architecture-agnostic, and works for both single- and multi-vector query embeddings; the KL-to-consensus-distribution formulation is clean and clearly presented (Algorithm 1, Figure 2).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: three ViDoRe benchmarks, 9 retriever pairs, comparisons against many hybrid baselines (RRF, rank/score aggregation, tuned variants), reranker comparisons, and latency/storage Pareto analyses. The efficiency story (up to ~14x faster and ~54x less memory than the strongest base model while matching quality) is a strong practical result.

Good breadth of analysis: hyperparameter sweeps over learning rate and steps, latency breakdown, ablations over candidate pool policy, loss function, role assignment, and extra search stage, plus zero-shot transfer to ViDoRe 3. Code is stated to be released.
Honest reporting of limitations, e.g., degradation on rare subsets for some models, ViDoRe 1 saturation, and cases where Qwen3 with GQR underperforms.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core idea (test-time query optimization via KL to a feedback distribution) is adapted from prior pseudo-relevance-feedback work (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025); the main contribution is replacing the cross-encoder feedback source with a complementary bi-encoder and applying it to multimodal retrieval, which is an incremental but useful extension.

Absolute gains are modest (roughly +1 to +4 NDCG@5 points, and near-zero on the saturated ViDoRe 1), and the analysis shows the effect is confined to the initial candidate pool; the paper provides no formal analysis or theoretical grounding for when/why the refinement helps.

Hyperparameter tuning is done per subset on a 10% development split of the same benchmark in the 'tuned' setting, which advantages tuned methods (including GQR) relative to a true zero-shot deployment; while zero-shot results are provided, more attention to sensitivity of results to tuning would strengthen the claims.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported, despite per-subset deltas that are sometimes small or negative; it is hard to judge robustness of the gains on individual subsets.

Evaluation is restricted to ViDoRe-family benchmarks and page-level document retrieval; no experiments on other multimodal retrieval settings (e.g., mixed-modality corpora, BEIR-style text tasks) that would demonstrate broader applicability of GQR.

Test-time optimization requires gradient access to the primary encoder's query embedding and extra per-query compute; the paper discusses latency but practical constraints (e.g., models that cannot expose gradients, or quantized serving) are not addressed.

strengths: The method is clearly presented: GQR refines the primary retriever's query embedding at test time via KL minimization toward a consensus distribution, and is architecture-agnostic across single- and multi-vector retrievers (Algorithm 1, Fig. 2).

Empirically thorough evaluation: 9 retriever pairs across ViDoRe 1/2/3, with comparisons to ranking-level (RRF, average ranking) and score-level fusion baselines, including tuned variants, plus Recall@5 checks.

Strong efficiency analysis: latency breakdowns (Fig. 5), latency-quality and storage-quality Pareto plots (Figs. 3, 9), and comparisons against a multimodal reranker (Table 11), supporting the headline 14x faster / 54x less memory claims.

Reasonable ablation coverage: hyperparameter sweeps over lr/T (Fig. 4), loss function variants (Table 18), candidate pool policy (Table 17), extra search stage (Table 16), role swapping (Table 19), and per-query dynamics analysis (Fig. 8).
The finding that a much weaker text retriever can still provide useful complementary signal through representation-level refinement is interesting and potentially useful for practitioners.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: test-time query optimization with pseudo-relevance feedback already exists (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025). The core change - replacing the cross-encoder teacher with a (possibly weaker) bi-encoder teacher and minimizing KL to a consensus distribution - is a fairly incremental modification, and the theoretical motivation in Sec. 2.4 is largely intuitive rather than rigorous.

Absolute gains are modest and noisy: average gains of +1.7 to +3.9 NDCG@5 points, with per-subset regressions in several cases (e.g., Qwen3 as complementary model harms Biomed Lectures by -2.4). No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported, which matters given benchmark sizes.

Fairness concerns in the tuned setting: GQR hyperparameters (lr, T) are tuned per subset on 10% dev splits, and GQR's tuning budget (6 lr values x 3 T values per subset) differs from the single scalar alpha tuned for the linear fusion baselines. A stronger, matched-budget baseline would be needed to attribute the gains to the representation-level mechanism rather than added tuning capacity.

The 'zero-shot' evaluation on ViDoRe 3 is only quasi zero-shot: the hyperparameter configuration was explicitly selected based on ViDoRe 2 results, so cross-benchmark generalization is partially compromised.

Scope is confined to visual document retrieval on ViDoRe-family benchmarks; ViDoRe 1 is saturated (near-ceiling, no gains), leaving essentially two benchmarks. There is no evidence the method transfers to other retrieval settings (e.g., general text-text hybrid retrieval or passage retrieval), weakening broader significance claims.

The mechanism-level claim that GQR exploits 'rich interactions' beyond score fusion is supported mainly by qualitative rank-trajectory visualizations (Fig. 8) rather than quantitative evidence that the observed gains stem from non-linear/geometric effects rather than implicit score reweighting.

The comparison to score fusion with tuned min-max normalization is close in places (e.g., +3.4% vs. GQR's +3.9% on ViDoRe 2), so the margin over the strongest simple baseline is thin relative to the added complexity (iterative gradient steps at query time).

strengths: The paper introduces GQR, a test-time query refinement method that transfers pseudo-relevance feedback ideas to hybrid multimodal retrieval by using a lightweight complementary bi-encoder instead of a heavy cross-encoder; this is a sensible and well-motivated contribution that fills a real gap between score-level fusion and full representation-level fusion.

The evaluation is broad and thorough: three ViDoRe benchmarks, 9 retriever pairs spanning both single-vector text models and multi-vector ColPali-style vision models, comparison against multiple well-known hybrid baselines (RRF, average ranking, min-max/softmax score aggregation) in both tuned and zero-shot settings, plus Recall@5 results in the appendix.

The efficiency analysis is a highlight: latency measurements on a fixed GPU, latency breakdown per component, storage-quality tradeoffs, and a comparison against cross-encoder rerankers convincingly show GQR sits on the latency-quality and memory-quality Pareto fronts (e.g., matching Llama-Nemo at ~14x speed and ~54x less memory).

Good ablation coverage: hyperparameter sweeps over learning rate and steps, candidate pool policy, extra search stage, loss function variants, and role swapping (primary vs. complementary), which strengthen the credibility of the design choices.
Zero-shot transfer to ViDoRe 3 using hyperparameters chosen on ViDoRe 2 partially mitigates concerns about overfitting the tuning, and the paper is candid about benchmark saturation on ViDoRe 1.
weaknesses: The core technique is an incremental combination of known ideas: test-time query optimization via KL-based pseudo-relevance feedback (Yu et al. 2021; Sung et al. 2023; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025) applied to a hybrid retrieval setting. The novelty lies mainly in the substitution of the feedback source (a weaker complementary bi-encoder) and the multimodal domain, which somewhat limits the conceptual contribution.

The absolute gains are modest and the margin over the strongest baseline is thin: on ViDoRe 2, GQR achieves +3.9% average gain versus +3.4% for tuned min-max score aggregation and +2.6% for tuned softmax aggregation. No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported, so it is unclear whether the ~0.5-1.3% improvement over tuned baselines is reliable, particularly given per-subset variance (Table 3 shows Std of 1.9).

All evaluation is confined to the ViDoRe benchmark family; there is no evidence of generalization to other document retrieval datasets (e.g., M2DV, MTEB-document variants) or to non-document retrieval tasks, which weakens the claimed broad applicability of the method.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is notable: GQR requires tuning both the learning rate and the number of steps per model pair (and per subset in the tuned setting), with degradation or instability at extreme values (Figure 4). This adds operational complexity relative to simple fusion baselines, and the tuned values (Tables 20-21) vary considerably across settings.

A small number of model-pair combinations show degradation (e.g., Qwen3 complementary with Colnomic on Economics/ESG subsets), and the paper's explanation of when the complementary signal helps vs. hurts remains qualitative rather than predictive.

The candidate pool construction (union of top-K from both retrievers) is itself a mild form of hybrid retrieval; although Table 17 shows the top-K-only variant performs comparably, this entangles the contribution of refinement per se with candidate expansion, and a cleaner decomposition would be reassuring.

The paper claims GQR 'matches the performance of models with significantly larger representations,' but the empirical gap between the best GQR hybrid and the strongest base model (Llama-Nemo) is within ~1.3 NDCG@5 points, and the Pareto claims rest on a single hardware configuration (A100) and one benchmark.
